newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu leaves Zaire dangerously divided.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu leaves Zaire dangerously divided.

text.p: President Mobutu Sese Seko's sudden return to France has left Zaire with potentially dangerous divisions within the army command and the political class, local commentators say.
Mobutu flew back to his French Riviera villa on Thursday, three weeks after returning home from months of cancer treatment and rest in Europe, reportedly to seek further medical attention.

During his brief stay in Zaire, Mobutu brought radical changes in the army. He shuffled out some close tribal and family relations accused of bleeding the army dry of resources, rendering it ineffective to face Rwandan-backed rebels who have seized a vast tract of territory since October.
However, experts on Zaire and military sources say he placed as many obstacles as advantages in the way of the new army command.

Under popular and international pressure, Mahele Lieko Bokungo, one of the rare generals who earned his stars on the battlefield instead of through family and ethnic ties to the president, was named army chief of staff.
In theory Mahele was given sweeping powers to bring to heel mutinous troops who fled the battlefront and to restructure Zaire's rag-tag army into a force capable of defending national territory.

But sources close to Mahele and experts say the general's powers are proving less than solid and Mobutu's tradition of neutralising potential adversaries has again proved stronger than the call for national interest.
"The general population, and international allies might want Mahele to succeed. However, no one else seems to," one Zaire expert said.

While some commentators consider the choice of a tough general with a reputation for discipline to head the army as protection against chaos should Mobutu die, others see Mahele already asphyxiated by the powerful interests of the presidential clique.
Should these interest groups retain their grip on the country's wealth and institutions, experts forecast a worsening of the crisis.
"While they can plough money in for the war effort from the diamond, petrol and transport sectors, they are not in a hurry to see the fighting end soon," a Western intelligence source said.

The source said for the moment Mahele is being prevented from assuming full control of the army, its weaponry, and vital information. In particular, they say, he does not control the best-equipped presidential and civil guards.
Mobutu, Zaire's ruler of 31 years, was heralded by his entourage as the one man capable of uniting the country and preventing it from falling apart after the rebel offensive in the east.
Well over 100,000 expectant inhabitants of the capital turned out to welcome Mobutu when he returned from France on December 17.
But by retaining a prime minister, Kengo wa Dondo, with little popular support and many enemies, Mobutu lost much of the initial support.
In defence of Mobutu, a senior government official said the president is no longer constitutionally empowered to make the sweeping changes Zaire needs.
"It is up to the government to pick up where Mobutu left off and...to take the kind of actions which will have an immediately positive impact on the misery of the population," the official said.
